title: Delhi Master Plan 2047 Approved With Push for Affordable Housing and Yamuna Restrictions
excerpt: The new two-decade plan targets 2 million new affordable dwelling units, tighter controls on Yamuna floodplain development, and mixed-use zoning to accommodate Delhi's growing population.
body:
• Delhi's new Master Plan 2047 has been cleared, replacing the previous 2041 plan with a longer planning horizon.
  • The plan targets approximately 2 million new dwelling units, including affordable rental housing and small-format homes of 40-60 square metres.
  • Tighter restrictions on Yamuna floodplain development aim to balance urban growth with river rejuvenation.
  • Mixed-use zoning and higher-density redevelopment in underused areas are key strategies to accommodate population growth.

Delhi has approved its new Master Plan 2047, setting the blueprint for the national capital's growth over the next two decades with a strong emphasis on affordable housing, tighter Yamuna floodplain restrictions, and mixed-use urban development to accommodate what is expected to be one of the world's most populous metropolitan areas.

The plan replaces the earlier Master Plan 2041 framework and extends the planning horizon to 2047, coinciding with the centenary of Indian independence. It addresses long-standing challenges around housing shortages, informal settlements, and environmental degradation that have defined Delhi's rapid but often chaotic urban expansion.

Affordable Housing at Scale

The plan targets approximately 2 million new dwelling units across multiple housing typologies, including affordable rental housing, small-format homes of 40-60 square metres, retirement communities, and serviced apartments for migrants and students. In greenfield areas, land will be acquired through pooling mechanisms designed to speed up development while ensuring orderly urban planning.

"The government also plans to incentivize private developers to build rental housing, acknowledging that home ownership remains out of reach for millions of Delhi residents."

For the large migrant population of working men and women, students, and informal sector workers who form a significant chunk of Delhi's economy, the plan proposes dormitories, hostels, and studio apartments. The government also plans to incentivize private developers to build rental housing, acknowledging that home ownership remains out of reach for millions of Delhi residents.

Yamuna Restrictions

The plan introduces tighter controls on development within the Yamuna floodplain, one of Delhi's most contested environmental zones. While the river is recognized as a prized urban asset, decades of encroachment, pollution, and unplanned construction have severely degraded its banks and water quality.

The new framework calls for protected zones along the Yamuna, with walking and cycling paths and restrictions on commercial and residential construction within the floodplain. However, urban planning experts have raised concerns about the impact on poor farmers and fishers who depend on the river for their livelihoods.

Redeveloping Underused Land

A key strategy in the plan is the redevelopment of underused and vacant government-owned land across the city. The plan identifies "a large proportion of underused land with a number of vacant sites as well as dilapidated built-up areas" that can be developed at higher densities to make optimum use of Delhi's limited land resources.

The plan also proposes that no new central government or public sector offices should be built within the National Capital Territory of Delhi, reflecting a long-term push to redistribute government infrastructure across the National Capital Region.

What It Means for NRI Investors

For diaspora investors with real estate holdings in Delhi-NCR, the new master plan is significant. Mixed-use zoning could unlock value in previously restricted areas, while the affordable housing push may create opportunities in a segment that has historically been underserved by organized developers. The Yamuna restrictions, meanwhile, could limit supply in certain zones, potentially supporting prices in areas that remain buildable under the new framework.
